screenshots.shows: Windows. Main widget, one row blocked on its user, one working and one finished, with the 5h and 7d usage bars in the header — the hero image on both the README and the docs index

steps: Windows. The macOS half of this figure is hero-macos, which is its own entry and its own script.

ENFORCED, not just asked for: the script calls Assert-Publishable before the shutter, which pipes /api/agents to lib/dashboard.py — the same list and the same rule the macOS scripts import. A row not on PUBLISHABLE_PROJECTS refuses the capture. Renames are covered: the check reads display_name as well as the project, because the rename is the string in the picture.

MORE ROWS NEXT TIME. The README prints this beside hero-macos in a two-column table, so the pair is read as one picture and their heights should be comparable. As of 2026-09-13 they are not: hero-macos was re-shot with seven rows (840x594, aspect 0.71) while this is three rows (634x283, aspect 0.45), so at equal column width the macOS side renders about 1.58x the height of this one and the row looks lopsided. Whenever this frame is next redone, stage enough sessions to land near the macOS aspect — roughly seven rows, and the sibling entry's note on leaving sync ON is how it got them, since a peer's rows count toward the picture and are worth showing. Nothing is wrong with the current frame on its own; this is only about the pair.
Deploy the current build so the shot matches the working tree, not the installed release

Stage a real spread: one session genuinely blocked on its user, one mid-turn, one finished. The dashboard's hook does not fire on PostToolUse, so a session busy inside a long turn does not refresh its row — the working row has to be one that is mid-turn right now.
Sessions live in public repositories only. A row's label is its actual prompt, and a private project's task text ends up in the frame verbatim.
Turn sync listening off (`sync.listen`, start-only) so a peer's rows are not in frame; the script refuses while a peer is connected.

Turn `restore_sessions` off and restart, so the widget starts empty and only the staged sessions get rows. With it on, every idle session the terminal can vouch for comes back and the frame is whatever happened to be running.

Both usage bars must have a reading. Restarting the app repeatedly trips the usage endpoint's 429 backoff and the bars then render `--%`; this is the only frame that shows the header, so wait for a poll that succeeds after the restarts.

Captured with -Method Alpha: the window is photographed over a black and a white backdrop and the alpha solved per pixel, so the frame carries the real border and rounded corners with everything outside them transparent. Do not add -Client; the script refuses the combination.

screenshots.shows: macOS. Main widget with seven rows — four local (one blocked on its user, one working, one finished, one idle) and three synced from a second machine, each carrying a device chip and a per-row token count — plus the 5h and 7d usage bars in the header; the hero image on both the README and the docs index

steps: macOS. The Windows half of this figure is hero-windows, which is its own entry and its own script.
Deploy the current build so the shot matches the working tree, not the installed release.

Stage a real spread: one session genuinely blocked on its user, one mid-turn, one finished. These are real sessions in real states — the script checks the spread and refuses rather than photographing three idle rows, which is the wrong picture that looks most plausible.

EVERY NAME AND EVERY PROMPT IN FRAME IS PUBLISHED. Outside compact view a row draws its task line, so this is the one figure that puts a session's real prompt on the README. The script refuses a project name not on `dash.PUBLISHABLE_PROJECTS` and prints every row's text before and after the shutter for the prose no list can vet — read that output before committing the frame.

A ROW RESTORED AFTER A RESTART HAS NO LABEL OF ITS OWN, and the widget then falls back to the last entry in its stored dialog. That is how a relayed agent-to-agent message reaches the picture verbatim, socket path and all: both `<cross-session-message from="uds:/tmp/cc-socks/<pid>.sock" …>` and `[cross-machine message, relayed by the dashboard] …` were in a probe of this frame on 2026-09-11. The fix is a fresh typed prompt in that session, which replaces the line; do not edit the stored dialog to tidy a screenshot.

SYNC IS DELIBERATELY LEFT ON for this frame, which is why the script is run with `--force`. The guard refuses while any row is synced from another machine, on the reasoning that a peer's rows put that machine's project names in the picture — true in general, and not here, where every peer row is already on `dash.PUBLISHABLE_PROJECTS`. Showing them is the point: cross-machine sync is a headline feature and a four-row local-only frame cannot depict it at all. Read the names before the shutter as always; `--force` skips the publishable check too, so that verification becomes manual.

Leave `restore_sessions` ON. It only takes effect at startup, so turning it off does nothing except empty the widget at the next restart — which, on 2026-09-13, is exactly what happened: it was turned off and the app restarted to apply it, destroying four rows whose labels had accumulated from real use. They came back only because the agterm tab titles still held their status glyphs and `session_restore` could rebuild from them. Do not restart this app to stage this frame unless something genuinely start-only requires it.

Both usage bars must carry a live reading. The script reads `usage_cache.json` from the app data dir and refuses when there is no stored sample or when `blocked_until` is still in the future — a bar with no reading draws a literal `--%`, and one replaying a stored sample behind an unexpired 429 draws at 55% opacity.

The compositor's drop shadow is out of the picture at source: `dash.capture_window` shoots with `screencapture -l<id> -o` and then runs `lib/trim_halo.py` itself, so a re-shoot has no trim step to remember.

Colour profile: a committed frame is sRGB. `screencapture` tags its output with the display's own profile — Color LCD here, a wide-gamut one — which stores the same colour as a different number; conversion to sRGB is the last step of `dash.capture_window`. Read a frame's tag back with `sips -g profile <png>`.

ROUNDED CORNERS, which the widget draws itself as of 2026-09-11 — see the compact-mode-macos entry for the four things that had to agree before `transparent: true` took effect. A capture should ramp 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 70, 255 down the diagonal, against 0, 0, 0, 64, 114, 255 on hero-windows, where Windows 11 rounds the window itself.

steps: Windows. The macOS half of this figure is compact-mode-macos.

Deploy the current build

The script writes `compact_mode`, captures, and puts it back. It writes the file whole and then touches it: the config watcher reads on the first notify event and debounces for 150ms, so a truncate-then-write hands it a half-written file and every setting silently falls back to its default.

This frame carries no device pill, because a peer's rows would put that machine's project names in the picture. The macOS variant is the one that shows sync, and it can: this device's own project names are public.

Captured with -Method Alpha: the window is photographed over a black and a white backdrop and the alpha solved per pixel, so the frame carries the real border and rounded corners with everything outside them transparent. Do not add -Client; the script refuses the combination.

screenshots.shows: macOS. Main widget in compact mode: seven rows, no label lines, showing IDLE/DONE/WORK/BLOCK badges and device pills on the three rows synced from another machine

steps: macOS. The Windows half of this figure is compact-mode-windows.
Deploy the current build

The script writes `compact_mode`, captures, and puts it back. It writes the file whole and then touches it past the config watcher's 150ms debounce, and a key config.json never held is restored by removing it rather than by writing `null` — a null field fails the parse for the whole file and every setting falls back to its default at once.

Have both local and synced rows live, so at least one device pill is in frame. The script refuses when no row is synced from another machine, and refuses any project name in frame that is not on the public list — `--publishable NAME ...` overrides that list for a project that really is public.
Capture the window rect

This frame was misfiled as a Windows capture until 2026-09-09. Two independent readings say otherwise: its device pills read CHROME, so the capturing machine is the other one; and its corner alpha ramp is byte-for-byte the shape terminal-tabs-macos has and hero-windows does not. The audit that got it wrong probed the top-left for macOS traffic-light hues, which cannot work on an undecorated window — it matched the DONE pill's green and nothing else.

ROUNDED CORNERS, which the widget draws itself as of 2026-09-11. The window is `decorations: false`, so macOS rounds nothing for it — the compositor rounds a titled window's frame — and it was square here while the same widget on Windows 11, which rounds the window itself, was round already. The fix is three things together and all three are required: `transparent: true` on the main window, `macOSPrivateApi: true` (the config doc says transparency on macOS needs it, and warns it bars the App Store, which costs nothing for a DMG and Homebrew build), and a `border-radius` with `overflow: hidden` on `.widget`. A fourth thing was overriding them all — `auto_resize::set_dark_window_background` re-set an OPAQUE `NSWindow.backgroundColor` at runtime, after the config, so `transparent: true` alone changed nothing; its alpha is now 0. A capture should ramp 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 70, 255 down the diagonal, against 0, 0, 0, 64, 114, 255 on the Windows half.

The compositor's drop shadow is out of the picture at source: `dash.capture_window` shoots with `screencapture -l<id> -o` and then runs `lib/trim_halo.py` itself, on both platforms, so a re-shoot has no trim step to remember.

Colour profile: a committed frame is sRGB. Output from `screencapture` is tagged with the display's own profile — Color LCD on this machine, a wide-gamut one — and the same colour is then stored as a less saturated number: re-tagging work-intensity-macos.png back to that profile moves its three title-bar lights from saturation 1.00 to 0.80, 0.74 and 0.72, against the 0.55 floor check-figures.py uses to recognise a macOS window by its traffic lights. This frame is the undecorated widget and has no lights for that check to read either way, but the conversion runs on every capture so that each committed frame's numbers mean the same thing. Conversion to sRGB is the last step of `dash.capture_window`, and the frame on disk carries that tag. Read it back with `sips -g profile <png>`.

screenshots.shows: Windows. Windows Terminal's tab strip, each tab carrying its session's status glyph written by the dashboard

steps: Windows. This is not the same picture as terminal-tabs-macos: there is no session sidebar on Windows, the same information rides the tab strip. The two are a pair for the feature, not for the UI, and the docs give each its own caption naming the application.

Assert-Publishable runs before the shutter, and its coverage here is PARTIAL by construction: it reads the dashboard's roster, so it covers every tab backed by a tracked session and cannot see a tab the dashboard knows nothing about — a shell, an editor, a session whose hook never fired. Read the strip by eye as well; the guard closes the common case, not all of it.

Stage the sessions in a terminal window of their own (`wt -w <name> new-tab`) so the strip carries only those tabs — every other tab open on the machine would otherwise be in frame, private names included
Several sessions across projects showing a spread of glyphs

The script hides the widget for the shot: it is always-on-top, and this is the one frame that has to be read off the desktop because PrintWindow returns a stale surface for Windows Terminal's XAML islands

Both crops are measured, not hardcoded — the strip's height from where the flat bar colour ends, and its width from the last tab before a long empty run, so the window controls at the far right stay out

EDGE: the script strokes the saved crop with the documentation skill's `hairline.py`, after the crop rather than before — a region crop brings no edge of its own, and this one kept the window's translucent border along its top and left while its right and bottom were bare content at (46, 46, 46), so on a dark page two sides had nothing to stop the picture. It is the same script the macOS captures call, so the two halves of this figure cannot drift apart in width or colour; it checks all four sides itself and declines a frame that already has a border, which is why the widget captures are untouched by it. Applied to the committed frame from the macOS side on 2026-09-12, so the file is correct now and a re-shoot on Windows keeps it.

The frame then ends on agterm's border and four rounded corners, where cropping a full-size window leaves the two right corners square; the script measures both and refuses the crop unless `--allow-cut` is given. The sidebar's width is read from agterm's own per-window state rather than assumed, and `--sidebar-width` is the way past a state file whose version it does not recognise.
Capture agterm's sidebar; the surrounding chrome is third-party and is not evidence for staleness
Fixed 2026-09-10 without a re-shoot: the blue bleed pixel at the top-left (RGB 57,142,198, alpha 9) was part of the corner halo and trim_halo.py cleared it.

Colour profile: a committed frame is sRGB. Output from `screencapture` is tagged with the display's own profile — Color LCD on this machine, a wide-gamut one — and the same colour is then stored as a less saturated number: re-tagging work-intensity-macos.png back to that profile moves its three title-bar lights from saturation 1.00 to 0.80, 0.74 and 0.72, against the 0.55 floor check-figures.py uses to recognise a macOS window by its traffic lights. screenshots.shows: macOS. History window for one session: timestamped prompts and replies with collapsed middles

steps: macOS. The Windows half of this figure is history-window-windows.
Deploy the current build

SUBJECT: the bga-assistant session (AnotherSava/bga-assistant, public), the same conversation history-window-windows photographs — the two variants are one figure and must not show two different sessions. The row id here is `bga-assistant`, the directory basename, since projects_root is unset on this machine; the Windows box calls the same checkout `assistant` and reaches the same title through a custom name, which is why the capture matches on the title rather than on the id.

SCROLL POSITION: set by `--height`, because the list is bottom-anchored and cannot be scrolled without driving the machine. There is deliberately no default for a committed capture — the script refuses one unless `--height` is passed explicitly, since the Windows 310 was measured against that machine's content and one line either way decides whether an absolute path is in frame or the <...> fold drops out of it. Hence the command above is the probe: run it, read the top edge and the tail, settle on a number, then run again with `--height N` and pin N here with what it was measured against.

KNOWN UNREACHABLE as of 2026-09-11, and not a tuning problem: the <...> fold this figure exists to show cannot be brought into frame at any window height for the fixed subject. Measured against the stored dialog — 470 entries held, nothing pruned — the most recent entry that folds is index 456, a 70-line 5721-char reply, thirteen entries from the end; every entry after it is under all three thresholds in `computeFold` (src/HistoryApp.svelte). The list opens at the bottom and /api/window exposes no scroll, so height is the only lever, and reaching entry 456 needs roughly twice the 923 logical px this display allows. The remedy is a long reply at the tail of that session, not a taller window.

The script opens History on `--session` and refuses an id the dashboard does not know. The session needs enough turns that at least one reply is folded behind a <...> button, and only its tail is in frame because the list opens at the bottom — read that tail first, from prompt_history.json in the app data dir, which is quicker to search than opening windows.
Probe with `--probe` until the height is right; a probe writes to tmp/ and cannot touch the committed frame.
Capture the history window rect

The frame on disk still carries the fully transparent one-pixel ring inside all four rounded corners, measured 2026-09-09: alpha 243, 163, 0, 99, 255 down the top-left diagonal, the 0 being the hole that makes the corners read ragged against a light page. It is the residue of trimming the compositor's drop shadow, and it is not a step anyone has to redo by hand — the re-shoot clears it by construction, measured on the re-shot work-intensity-macos frame as a ramp of 0 … 0, 99, 255 with no hole.

screenshots.shows: Windows. Work intensity window, Days view, one week of 10-minute token bars with each row's active time, tokens and share of the weekly quota in the right margin, under a native Windows title bar

steps: SUBJECT: the week of Aug 31 – Sep 6, 2026. Pinned by date (-WeekStart), not by the -Offset the window's API takes, because an offset is relative to the run date and would photograph a different week every week while looking like a constant. A re-shoot keeps this week: work-intensity-macos shows the same week, which is what makes the pair two pictures of one thing.
Windows. The macOS half of this figure is work-intensity-macos.
Deploy the current build

1520 logical px wide, and that is about the plot rather than the header now: the Navigation and Legend hints are gone and what is left fits on one line at the window's own 1000px default, so the old collide-below-1280 / wrap-at-1320 thresholds describe nothing. The width buys horizontal resolution — 144 ten-minute slots across the plot, and the shape of a day is what the figure argues.
The script parks the mouse pointer clear of the window: hovering a bar raises a tooltip that then sits in the committed frame

The script places the window at the top-left of the PRIMARY display before sizing it, and `Assert-Rendered` refuses the frame if the right edge came back opaque black. Both exist because the first end-to-end run of this script found the chart on a 1440-wide portrait monitor and committed a 1522px frame whose last 239px were a black band: a Windows capture reads the window's surface, so the part hanging off a display returns unrendered rather than missing, at the full window size.

Frame size is unchanged at 2284x1097, 144dpi — 1520 logical px on the 150% primary display. A run that finds it 1522x732 has shot it on a 100% monitor, which is the wrong one: at that size the plot has two thirds of the horizontal resolution the 144 ten-minute slots need.

Header contents as shot: one scope ("This week:" in Days, "Week average:" in Weeks) over Active / Tokens / Quota, with Active rounded to whole hours. The Navigation and Legend hints that used to sit right of the totals are gone, and the ← → buttons keep reserved slots either side of the date so nothing moves when the view switches.
